memories.memory_text: I was in the room with the neurologist, who told me about my wife's condition—she shows minimal and inconsistent responses, reacting non-purposefully to stimuli, with primitive reflexes that don't change much no matter what's happening around her.

grounded_facts: A scheduled meeting between Matt and a neurologist to discuss the neurological status of Matt's wife.
memories.memory_text: I had a scheduled meeting with the neurologist to discuss the current state of my wife's neurological condition, sitting across from him as he delivered the findings.

grounded_facts: The neurologist conveys the clinical observations about Matt's wife's neurological responses.
memories.memory_text: The neurologist shared the clinical observations about my wife's neurological responses, describing how she reacts in a non-specific way to stimuli, sometimes with brief specific reactions, but mostly with the same primitive reflexes regardless of what's presented.

grounded_facts: Matt recalls past accusations from his wife, drawing a personal parallel to the clinical description he is hearing.
memories.memory_text: I remembered how Elizabeth used to accuse me of being unresponsive and mechanical, and it struck me that the way the doctor described her condition felt like a cruel echo of those old arguments.

grounded_facts: Matt realizes he may have to decide whether to continue life support for Liz, but recalls she has a living will, which means she has already made the decision.
memories.memory_text: I realized I might have to decide whether to keep Liz on life support, but then I remembered she has a living will—she already made that choice herself.

memories.memory_text: I was told by Noe that Scottie's teacher was calling with an urgent matter, and I knew I had to take the call.

memories.memory_text: I said I thought keeping Scottie in her normal routine might help her, and I admitted I wouldn’t really know how to handle her at home since I’m already overwhelmed and she’d probably rather be with her friends or people who know more about kids.

memories.memory_text: I was in a meeting with Ms. Hayashi and Mrs. Thull about Scottie’s photos upsetting her classmates, and they told me how some kids went home disturbed and parents were angry.

grounded_facts: Matt denies engaging Scottie in emotional conversations about the family crisis, despite claiming otherwise, revealing his avoidance of difficult emotional discussions.
memories.memory_text: I told Mrs. Thull that I’ve been talking with Scottie about what’s going on and helping her express her feelings, but the truth is, I haven’t really had those conversations — I just said yes because it was easier than admitting I don’t know how to handle it.

grounded_facts: Ms. Hayashi verbally reprimands Scottie for her inappropriate singing and behavior outside the classroom.

memories.memory_text: I hesitated when Scottie was acting out, not stepping in right away, and only told her to knock it off after Ms. Hayashi reprimanded her first, which reminded me how I tend to hold back in these moments.

grounded_facts: A school activity where students present personal artwork, in this case involving Scottie's photographs of her ill mother.
memories.memory_text: There was a school activity where students presented personal artwork, and it was during this that Scottie included photographs of her ill mother, which led to our confrontation.

grounded_facts: Scottie defends her artistic decision by referencing a famous photographer who documented her mother's illness.
memories.memory_text: I remember Scottie defending her art project by saying she was inspired by a famous photographer who documented her mother's illness, claiming that's what she was doing too.

memories.memory_text: I told Scottie she should talk to her mother because it might help Elizabeth hear that she’s still loved and could even help her wake up sooner, and I wanted her to express her feelings too.

grounded_facts: Scottie specifies her drink preference when Matt offers to get her something.

memories.memory_text: I heard Barb threaten to report Scottie to the headmaster if she didn't apologize to Lani.

memories.memory_text: I remembered how Lani once locked Scottie out during her birthday party, and I brought it up to show that these things happen on both sides.

memories.memory_text: I stepped in when Barb accused Scottie of not being sorry, reminding everyone that kids can be mean but they grow out of it, and I recalled how Lani once locked Scottie out during a birthday party just to show off, trying to show that one act doesn't capture who someone really is.

memories.memory_text: I visited Lani's house with Scottie at dusk, and we had a brief interaction with Barb Higgins before leaving.

memories.memory_text: I asked Scottie if she would act differently around Lani, and she told me it was hard because Lani has a face you just want to hit.

memories.memory_text: I had a solitary moment looking up at the portraits of Edward and Margaret, thinking about what it means to carry on—or let go of—this inherited status and wealth.

memories.memory_text: I was told by Noe that my cousins had arrived at my office.

memories.memory_text: When I opened the curtain, I found something unexpected instead of the corpse I thought would be there.

memories.memory_text: I saw Kai apply lipstick and blush to Elizabeth's face to help her look less pale and more presentable.

memories.memory_text: I decided to get her something to eat and said, 'What else is new? Let's get you something to eat.'

memories.memory_text: I cut off Troy when he asked about Elizabeth's condition and told him to go be with his friends, that we should just leave it alone.

memories.memory_text: I remember Cousin Hugh pressing me to sign the sale document, implying there would be consequences if I refused, even saying they’d come after me legally, but reminding me we’re family.

grounded_facts: Matt delivers an impassioned speech about the family's cultural connection to the land and his duty as trustee.
memories.memory_text: I gave a speech about how, despite our haole ways, we still carry Hawaiian blood and are tied to this land, and I feel a duty to protect it for our children.

grounded_facts: A gathering of forty King cousins to conduct a poll on the sale of family land, involving ballots placed in a calabash.
memories.memory_text: I was there when the forty King cousins gathered to vote on selling the family land, and I saw the ballots go into the calabash, but I knew I couldn't let it happen — I'm the trustee, and I refused to sign.

grounded_facts: Matt, as trustee, declares he will not sign the document authorizing the sale of the family land, reversing expected approval.
memories.memory_text: I declared I wouldn’t sign the sale document as trustee, stating I have seven years to figure out how to keep the land and that I’m not going to be the one to end our family’s connection to it.

grounded_facts: The family gathers in the hospital room as Elizabeth nears death, maintaining a constant presence.
memories.memory_text: I remember how we were all gathered around Elizabeth in the hospital room, holding our ground as a family in those final moments.

grounded_facts: Julie Speer arrives at the hospital with flowers to visit Elizabeth, expressing that she felt compelled to come because her husband did not.
memories.memory_text: I saw Julie Speer come into the room with flowers, and she told us she felt she should stop by because she'd been thinking about us and knew my mom was there.

grounded_facts: Julie tells Matt that she learned about the affair from Brian after smelling alcohol and noticing his strange behavior.
memories.memory_text: Julie told me she learned about the affair after Brian came home acting strange and she smelled alcohol on him, and that she eventually got the truth out of him.

grounded_facts: Julie speaks to the unconscious Elizabeth, expressing forgiveness but also naming the harm caused.
Julie speaks to the unconscious Elizabeth, declaring that she forgives her for trying to take Brian and for nearly destroying her family.
memories.memory_text: I watched Julie speak to Elizabeth while she lay unconscious, and I heard her say she forgave her—for trying to take Brian and for nearly destroying her family—even though she wanted to hate her; I let her have that moment, but then I stepped in and told her it was enough.

grounded_facts: Matt tells Julie that Brian did not truly love Elizabeth, offering her some emotional relief.
memories.memory_text: I told Julie that Brian didn't really love Elizabeth, just so she'd know the truth and maybe find some peace.

grounded_facts: After Julie leaves, Matt realizes this is his moment to say farewell to Elizabeth, and he does so with physical intimacy and emotional words.
memories.memory_text: After Julie left, I realized it was my moment to say goodbye to Elizabeth, so I held her and spoke from the heart, saying, 'Goodbye, my love, my friend, my pain, my joy. Goodbye.'

grounded_facts: Alexandra exits Elizabeth's room with a distant sadness, indicating emotional distress after a private moment.
memories.memory_text: I saw Alexandra come out of Elizabeth's room with a distant sadness on her face, and it struck me how deeply she was hurting after that private moment.

grounded_facts: Matt and Sid rise to comfort Alexandra; she allows brief hugs but is emotionally distant.
memories.memory_text: I rose with Sid to comfort Alexandra, and though she allowed me to hug her briefly, I could feel how emotionally distant she was, not really letting us in.

grounded_facts: Alexandra signals Matt to let her handle Scottie's entry into Elizabeth's room.
memories.memory_text: I saw Alexandra signal me to step back, letting her take charge of getting Scottie into Elizabeth's room.

grounded_facts: Alexandra takes Scottie into Elizabeth's room, providing reassurance to her fearful sister.
memories.memory_text: I watched Alexandra take Scottie into Elizabeth's room, reassuring her as she guided her fearful sister inside.

grounded_facts: Matt signals Alexandra to proceed with scattering the ashes.
memories.memory_text: I gave Alexandra the go-ahead when she looked to me, letting her know it was okay to start scattering the ashes.

grounded_facts: Alexandra tells Scottie how to say goodbye to her mother.
memories.memory_text: I heard Alexandra tell Scottie to just say goodbye to her mother.

grounded_facts: Matt encourages Scottie to proceed with scattering the ashes.
memories.memory_text: I told Scottie it was okay and encouraged her to go ahead and scatter the ashes.

grounded_facts: After scattering the ashes, Matt and his daughters place their leis into the water as a symbolic gesture.
memories.memory_text: After we scattered Elizabeth's ashes, I took off my lei and placed it into the water, and my daughters did the same as a final tribute.

grounded_facts: A family ritual at sea where Elizabeth's ashes are scattered into the ocean.
memories.memory_text: I was there with the girls as we scattered Elizabeth's ashes into the ocean, and I remember saying, 'Well, here we are, just the four of us. For the last time,' before I had Alexandra start, giving her the go-ahead when she looked to me, then pouring the rest into the sea and placing my lei in the water too.

grounded_facts: The family scatters Elizabeth's ashes into the ocean during a ceremonial farewell.
memories.memory_text: I gave Alex the go-ahead, and then I poured the rest of Elizabeth's ashes into the ocean, taking off my lei and placing it in the water as the girls followed my lead.

memories.memory_text: I heard Dad’s voice outside the dorm supervisor’s room, asking to take me, like he had to come get me in the middle of the night because everything was falling apart.
I was laughing because Dad showing up in his coat on the soccer field was so ridiculous — I couldn’t believe he actually came all the way out here.
When he said I had to come home to see Mom, I threw my golf club into the dark — I don’t even know where it went — and just yelled, 'Fuck Mom!'
I asked Matt how long I had to stay, because I could already feel the walls closing in and I didn’t owe him a performance just for showing up.
I told him I was going swimming—not waiting for permission, not looking back—because the only thing worse than this family breakfast was sitting through more fake concern.
I told Dad, 'You really don't have a clue, do you? Dad, she was cheating on you.' The words came out sharp, like breaking glass. I couldn't believe he still didn't get it.
I told him I saw her go into the house with that guy, his hand on her ass, and how it made me sick. I remember how quiet he got—like the air got sucked out of the room.
I looked at Dad and said, 'Dad, this is Sid,' like it was obvious he needed to know who Sid was, even if he didn’t want to.
When Dad tried to brush Sid off, I told him, 'Sid's coming with us, okay?'—not asking, just stating it, because I wasn’t going to let him decide who I could be around.
I told Dad that Sid knows everything, standing right there with Matt approaching the car, and I meant it—he’s part of this now, no matter how much Dad wants to control who’s in the loop.
I asked Gramps if he was okay when he tossed the papers and stared off like he was somewhere else—I could see he was unraveling, and someone had to say something.
I didn't tell Mom I got my period for almost a year because she always wanted me to act older, and when it finally happened, I thought I'd shat myself.
I asked if I should go ring the bell, just to see what would happen, but Matt shut it down fast.
Before that, I told them we should Google Brian Speer later—something concrete to do instead of just sitting there staring at that sad little house.
I saw Brian Speer’s face on that real estate sign and told Dad to go back — I knew it was him the second we passed.
I got out of the car and took a photo of his face on the flyer — needed proof, and no one else was going to do it.

I told Mom I was sorry for being bad, for wasting her money on private schools, for everything — and then Matt spanked me. I couldn’t believe it, standing there in the hospital room, and all I could say was, 'Did you just spank me?'

After the spanking, I leaned in and told Mom I always wanted to be like her — that I *am* like her, exactly like her — even if it sounded dramatic. I meant it, even if I couldn’t say it without sarcasm.

I stood in the doorway and told Dad to drop it, that he had bigger things to deal with than chasing down Brian Speer. I asked if he was recording, not because I cared about the deposition, but because I couldn’t believe he was focusing on work at a time like this.

After seeing the look on Dad’s face—like he actually had a plan for once—I said I wanted to go too. When he tried to shut me down, I shot back, 'Fuck that. Let's all get out of town,' because sitting around pretending everything was normal was worse than whatever mess we’d drive into.
Cousin Ralph nodded at me without knowing my name, just another face in the family he can't be bothered to remember.
I told Dad I stopped using because boarding school made it impossible to get anything — no big deal, just how it went.
I cut in because the conversation was getting too soft, too fake—mimicking Scottie, telling Matt to stop babying her, just shut it all down.
I told Scottie Reina’s a fucked-up ho-bag and he needs to stay away from her—she’s going to end up a meth-head, used by stupid guys. I made him say it: she’s a twat.
When Scottie said he wanted to end up like me, I had to clarify—I meant the earlier me, the one who was mean and yelled at Mom. I didn’t want him to confuse who I am now with who I used to be.

I watched my dad talk to that woman from a distance, standing there pretending to just be looking at the water, but I knew he was trying to find something out. When he said Hugh King was his cousin and she mentioned Brian Speer, I could see it hit him—like he was holding back something heavy.

I remember pushing Dad to act right then—'So let's do it right now. Let's go knock on his door'—and feeling that sharp rush of satisfaction when he agreed, like we were finally moving instead of just talking.

I called Sid over and told them the plan—Dad and I would go talk to the Holitzers while they took Scottie back to the hotel, and I remember how fast Sid shut down Scottie's protest with a joke about TV.
I told Matt, 'Don't be a pussy,' right before we walked up to Julie Speer. He was freezing, stammering about what to say, and I couldn't let him blow this.
I saw Julie come out with hamburger patties and elbowed Matt hard—this was the moment, no backing out. I didn't speak then, but I made sure he moved forward.
I cut Sid off when he started talking about exposing the affair just to make himself feel righteous—he wasn’t thinking about Scottie at all.
I stood up and said my dad’s been doing an amazing job, because no one else was going to say it while Grandpa Scott tore into him right here in Mom’s room.

I felt Matt and Sid step toward me, arms open, but I didn’t want it—I let them hug me for a second anyway, just to get through it. My body was heavy, like I was walking through water, and all I could think was that Scottie still hadn’t seen her.

I crouched slightly to meet Scottie’s eyes, then held out my hand—she looked so small, so scared. I guided her toward the room, saying something soft, something steady, even though my chest felt like it was cracking open.
I sat down next to Matt, pulled the quilt over my legs, and asked for some ice cream. He didn’t say anything, just handed me his bowl without looking away from the TV.

memories.memory_text: I sat there with my papers spread around me, looking up at Elizabeth—her body stiff in that bed, tubes in her nose and throat, machines breathing for her—and I said her name out loud, like I was trying to make it real: this is Elizabeth King, my wife.

I sat there listening to the neurologist describe Elizabeth’s reflexes as primitive and inconsistent, and all I could think was how she used to say I was the one who reacted without purpose, going through the motions.
I yanked the phone from Scottie’s hands after she refused to tell me what she’d said to her mother — all that giggling while her mom lies there unconscious, it made me snap.
I just want to be a normal guy — not another link in this chain of ancestors staring down from the walls, their lives dictating mine.

I sat there across from Dr. Johnston, hearing him say the words — no eye movement, no brainstem reflexes, she'll never be like she was — and I just stayed still, not moving, like if I didn’t react, it wouldn’t be true.

Troy approached our table, asking about Elizabeth with this intense, personal concern—saying he'd visited her, that her hand moved when he spoke, like it meant something. I stared him down because something about the way he said it, like he was close to her, set me off.

After Troy left, Scottie snapped at him—comparing Mom's twitches to a dead chicken running around—and then just got up and walked away. I watched her go, and I didn’t even look back at Troy; I just followed her, feeling how alone we both were in it.

I found Alexandra laughing in the moonlight, drunk with a golf club in her hand, acting like it was all a big joke—her friend had just fallen in the grass with a bottle, and she kept saying 'My fucking dad is here!' like it was the funniest thing.

When I told her she needed to come home to see her mother, she didn't say anything—just threw her golf club into the dark and screamed 'Fuck Mom!'—and I just stood there, hearing my own voice in my head asking why the women in my life keep falling apart.

Alexandra told me, 'Dad, she was cheating on you,' and said she saw Mom go into a house with some guy who had his hand on her ass. I couldn't process it—kept asking if she was sure, what it meant, who the man was, but she didn't know.
After she told me everything, I stood up, walked in a circle, didn't know where to go or what to do—then I just said, 'Watch Scottie,' like that was the only thing I could hold onto.
I was walking away when Mark called out the name—Brian Speer. Two e's. That detail stuck, like it made it more real, more permanent.

I pulled the car over across from that ordinary house and just stared at it—plain walls, no fence, nothing remarkable—and asked, 'There? He lives there?' It didn't look like a place that could break my life apart.

I sat there with the engine off, feeling the weight of what we were doing—crouching when a plumbing truck passed, debating whether to ring the doorbell—and then finally started the car, saying, 'Okay, that's enough. We're getting out of here,' because staying felt pointless and degrading.
I crouched by her bed and asked her if she was really going to leave me for Brian Speer—called her a liar, told her she was still ruining everything, even lying there on a ventilator.

I picked up her childhood doll and threw it, muttering 'Daddy's little girl'—suddenly disgusted by the things they'd brought to make her seem innocent, while I was left holding the truth no one else knew.

I stood in the living room and told everyone that Elizabeth wasn't going to make it, that we were taking her off life support the next day — her wishes — and I could feel my voice breaking as I said I wanted to tell them in person.
I asked Alex if she’d been using drugs, and she shot me a look before stomping out her cigarette—then admitted she’d stopped, mostly because boarding school cut off her access.
After she admitted the truth, I told her I was proud—she’s here helping with Scottie and me, and that meant something, even if she brushed it off.
I saw sand stuffed in Scottie’s bikini top and told her to take it out—Alex and Sid didn’t stop her, and I had to be the one to say something, again.

I was jogging at dawn along Hanalei Bay, out of breath and pushing through the burn, when I saw a man in a Stanford Lacrosse shirt coming toward me — and something in his stride or the set of his shoulders made me slow, then stop, then turn around to follow.

I kept muttering under my breath, 'Hi, you don't know me, but I know you,' over and over, like I was rehearsing it, and when I finally said it out loud — 'Hi, I'm Liz's husband' — he just looked at me and said 'That's right. Fuckface' before walking away.
I was ready to confront him, but then I saw the woman in the white bathing suit and the two little boys come out — he has a family, just like me. I couldn't do it then.
I told Brian Speer to his face that Elizabeth is dying — that we’d taken her off the machines that morning and she’d be gone in a few days. I said it flat, no warning, just the truth.
I watched his face freeze when I said her name — Brian’s grin dropped the second I mentioned Elizabeth. Alexandra and I looked at each other, then back at him, letting it sink in.
I pushed Brian to tell me how it started—Super Bowl party at the Mitchells’—and I kept pressing because I needed to know what made someone cross that line, even if he said it just happened.
I asked if he’d ever been in my bedroom, and when he said once, I felt a sharp sting—there was no reason for him to be in there, and I couldn’t believe she let him.

Scott Thorson walked in and started grilling me about the land deal right there in the hospice room, as if Elizabeth wasn't lying in the bed, as if this was the time or place. When he implied I was profiting from her accident, I could feel my hands tighten — I told him she deserved more, because I couldn't say anything else without breaking down.
I sat at my desk in the silence, just the clock ticking past 3:20, staring at the blueprints and renderings spread out like a verdict I couldn’t escape.

I remember sitting at the table with Hugh and Six, watching the calabash go around, each cousin dropping in their ballot like it was some sacred ritual, and realizing none of us had earned that land—it was entrusted, not earned.
I remember Hugh handing me the pen, smiling like it was all settled, and I said no—I said I wouldn't sign, and I saw the look on his face, like I'd broken some unspoken rule.

Julie Speer stood by Elizabeth's bed and said she forgave her—for trying to take Brian, for almost destroying her family—and I didn't know what to do, so I just stood there, then told her it was enough, that she should stop.

After Julie left, I realized it was the last time I'd be alone with Elizabeth, so I took her hand, touched her hair, kissed her lips, and whispered goodbye—over and over—like I was finally letting her go.
I told Alex to go first, and I watched her hesitate, holding the scoop of ashes like she was afraid to let go—then she poured them in, and we all just stared as the water darkened and swallowed them.
After Scottie said goodbye, I took the box, looked down at what was left of Elizabeth, and poured the rest into the sea—then I dropped my lei in, feeling the weight lift just enough to breathe.
I handed Scottie her ice cream and got under the quilt with her.
Alex came in, saw the show, sat down beside me, and asked for some. Without looking away from the screen, I passed her my own ice cream. We just sat there, the three of us, as the credits rolled.

dialogue_exemplars: My friends on the mainland think just because I live in Hawai'i, I live in paradise. Like a permanent vacation -- we're all just out here drinking mai-tais, shaking our hips, and catching waves. Are they nuts? How can they possibly think our families are less screwed up, our heart attacks and cancers less fatal, our grief less devastating? Hell, I haven't been on a surfboard in fifteen years.
For the last 23 days, I've been living in a "paradise" of IVs and urine bags and endotracheal tubes and six-month-old US magazines. Paradise. Paradise can go fuck itself.

Somehow it feels natural to find a daughter of mine on a different island. A family seems exactly like an archipelago -- all part of the same geographic expression but still islands -- separate and alone, always drifting slowly apart.

People will be relieved, Hugh, the whole state. I sign that document, it's over. End of the line. Something that was ours to protect will be gone. Even though we're haole as shit and go to private schools and clubs and can't even speak pidgin, let alone Hawaiian, we still carry Hawaiian blood, and we're still tied to this land. And ourchildren are tied to this land. It's a miracle that for whatever bullshit reason 150 years ago, we own this much of... paradise, but we do. And for whatever bullshit reason now, I'm the trustee. And I'm not signing. And if you sue me, it'll only make us closer.
Goodbye, Elizabeth. Goodbye, my love, my friend, my pain, my joy. Goodbye. Goodbye. Goodbye.

I almost told you yesterday. She's
never going to wake up. It's for sure
now. You hear me? We're pulling the
plug. You were putting lipstick on a
corpse.

My missionary ancestors came to the
islands and told the Hawaiians to put
on clothes, work hard, believe in
Christ, and stop surfing and hula
dancing. They made business deals
along the way -- buying an island, or
marrying a princess and inheriting her
land. Now their descendants wearbikinis and running shorts, play beach
volleyball and surf, and take up hula
dancing. Hawai'i has always been a
place of contradiction.

Elizabeth's going to make it out okay. I know it. It's not her time yet. She'll wake up, Scottie and Alexandra will have their mother back, and we'll talk about our marriage. I'll sell the land and quit my practice and buy her whatever she wants -- a big boat, a house in France, a trip around the world, just the two of us. We'll get close again, like the early days. It's still in us. It must be.

We were on Moloka'i with Mark and Kai,
and your mom was out surfing and saw a
shark right beneath her on a wave.
Like right beneath her. She got down
on her stomach and started paddling
like crazy, and this big fin keptfollowing her. She even paddled up
onto the nearest rocks instead of all
the way to shore. Got cuts all over
her legs and hands. Only time I ever
saw your mother scared, and she was
really scared. She even threw up.
Crying and shaking. I had to hold her
for a long time. She really thought
she was going to die. Of course she
hid all that from the Mitchells, turned
it into a funny "Me-versus-a-shark"
story. I told her...

What is it about me that makes women in
my life want to destroy themselves? Elizabeth with her motorcycles and
speedboats and alcoholism.
On the phone he can escape. In person he has nowhere to go. I want to see his face. I want to change his life.
Take a good look, girls. In the old days, this was part of your great-great grandmother's inheritance going all the way back to Kamehameha I.

The whole goddamned state is following
my decision on who's going to buy
,000 acres on Kaua'i my family has
owned since the 1860s. My cousins and
I meet in six days to approve a buyer.
Ever since my father died nine
ago, I'm the sole trustee, the
controlling trustee, so I hold all the
cards. Why does so much have to dependon me -- my wife, my daughters, my
family's land? I just want to hide.

My great-great-grandmother was Princess
Margaret Ke'alohilani, one of the last
direct descendants of King Kamehameha.
She was originally supposed to marry
her hanai brother, but she fell in love
with her haole banker and estate
manager, Edward King, whose parents
were missionaries.

Unlike a lot of my cousins, I haven't touched my share of the trust money. Like my father before me, I live only on the income from my law practice. I don't want my daughters growing up entitled and spoiled. And I agree with my father -- you give your children enough money to do something but not enough to do nothing.

memories.memory_text: I was dancing outside the classroom, singing 'This shit is bananas' over and over with my earbuds in, and I didn’t even notice Dad or the teachers looking at me.
I told Dad I'm a real photographer, just like that famous lady who took pictures of her mom in the hospital, and that's what I'm doing for my art project.

I didn’t know what to say to Mom, so I just said I was hungry and wanted a Sprite — not diet, regular — and Matt had to drag me to the chair, but he kept pushing me to talk or write her something, like a letter, even though she’s in a coma and can’t read it.
I remember Matt saying, 'Elizabeth's going to make it out okay,' like he really believed it — like Mom was gonna wake up and everything would just fix itself.
I told Dad it was private, and he got so mad—he even grabbed my phone, but I wasn’t gonna say what I said to Mom. It was just for her.

I saw those Melnick dorks walking with their stupid kayaks and matching shirts, and I just had to say it—'Dorks!'—and then laughed because it was so obvious they were dorks, and even Matt couldn't stop me from saying it twice.
I remember sitting outside Lani's house all day after she locked me out of her birthday party, while everyone else was inside having fun.
I said 'Sorry' real quick, then nodded super big when Dad pushed me to show I meant it, even though I didn't feel sorry at all.
I asked Dad why it's called a jellyfish when it's not a fish and not jelly. I said I'm going to ask Mom when she wakes up.
I told Troy that just because Mom's hand moved doesn't mean she's getting better — it's like a chicken running after its head's cut off, still dead.
I said I hated him, but then I told Dad I didn't mean to say the thing about the dead chicken. I just got scared 'cause I don't want Mom to die.
Dad said we should drive to the airport and surprise Alex on the Big Island, and I said yeah—she should come home, and I'm out of school anyway.
I flipped off Troy as Matt and I walked away — I didn’t even think, I just did it, my hand popping up like it had its own mind.
I was so tired, just leaning against the wall when Matt knocked on the door to get Alex. I didn’t say much, but I remember the TV was still on in the background and I could barely keep my eyes open.
I ran up and yelled, 'Hi, Alex! It's me, Scottie!' and then I told her we came to get her to come home — I haven't been to school in three whole days.
I said I don't like eggs when Matt brought them to me, and then I told him I thought they were for him, not me.
When Matt said they shouldn't talk in front of me, I said 'I don't mind' — I wanted them to know I can handle it.
I ran out in just my bra and panties, and when Matt told me to go change, I flipped him off and ran back inside.
I was laughing with Alex and Sid in the pool chairs, feeling good in my dumb shirt, until Dad showed up and everything got all stiff and serious.
They were talking about taking me to a movie, like I didn’t hear them saying it was to get me out of the house.

Cousin Ralph said my name, sort of, when he saw us at the airport, but I think he forgot it right after — he called me something else, maybe Alex? I waved anyway because he was smiling and looked like he knew Dad.
I took my shoes off and slid across the super shiny floor—it was so slick, like ice, but warm. I giggled when I almost crashed into the big plant.
I put sand in my bikini top and called them my beach boobs, but then Dad saw and got mad, and Mom and Sid told me to take them out, so I stomped to the water pulling it all out.
I asked Dad if we could swim with sharks in a cage like in the hotel magazine, but Mom shut me down fast, saying we weren't here for stuff like that.
I asked Dad how he and Mom met, and if he thought she was pretty, and what he loved about her—my voice felt shaky even though I tried to sound casual, and then Alex snapped at me to shut up.
I grabbed the remote and saw those movie ads with women in sexy clothes — I said, 'Let's watch one of these!' just to see what would happen.
Alexandra told me to say 'twat,' so I did — then I started running around yelling it over and over, 'Twat, twat, twat, twat!' like it was a game.
I was sleeping in the window seat on the plane, so I don’t remember anyone talking about me, but I can sort of feel them looking over.
Dr. Herman handed me a little rubber octopus that squeaked, and said it was smart like a dog and used ink to hide from danger.
I asked if Mom was getting better because she wasn't on any machines, and no one answered — they just looked at each other.
